topic.title: Environment: Origins and daily operation in River Restoration Projects
topic.focus: how the initiative began and how it works each day

candidate_instructions: Read all five sections. Answer Questions 1-25. Follow the stated word limits exactly.

sections.heading: The weir at Colònia Nova
sections.text: The mill at Colònia Nova, on the River Ter about twenty kilometres north of Vic, stopped weaving in 2011. Its weir, built in 1898 to drive the turbines, stayed where it was. In the spring of 2013 a science teacher at the local secondary school, Jordi Puig, sent his fourteen-year-olds out with thermometers as an ordinary class exercise. The water immediately above the weir turned out to be almost four degrees warmer than the water below it, and the pupils found no trout at all in the slack pool behind the wall. Puig had expected neither result. He wrote to the town council, received a polite reply, and then wrote again every month for a year. The association now known as Riu Viu was registered in 2014, largely because a permit application needed the signature of a legal body.

sections.heading: Eight o'clock at the bridge
sections.text: Riu Viu's week is organised around a gauge painted on the second pier of the Pont de Sant Roc. Every morning at eight, one of the volunteers reads it and posts the figure to a group message, and the same figure is copied by hand into a ledger kept in the old mill office. That number then decides what happens. Below 40 centimetres, planting is possible on the exposed gravel; above a metre, nobody enters the channel at all. Between November and January, while the trout are spawning, no work is done on the river bed whatever the gauge says. Volunteers describe this rule as inconvenient and observe it anyway. The eight o'clock reading has been missed on only nine mornings since March 2015.

sections.heading: Saturday parties
sections.text: The association employs two people: a coordinator, Marta Serra, and a part-time river ecologist. Everything else is done by roughly sixty volunteers, of whom perhaps twenty-five appear in any given month. Work parties meet on Saturday mornings from March to October. Their main task is cutting giant cane, an invasive reed that colonises the banks and crowds out the willow that shades the water. A party of fifteen can clear about 200 metres of bank in a morning, and the same stretch has to be revisited twice more before the roots give up. New volunteers are not sent on a training course. They are put beside somebody who has done the work before, which is how most of what Riu Viu knows is passed on.

sections.heading: What the arrangement costs
sections.text: The work is paid for out of about 310,000 euros a year. Rather more than half of that comes from a clearance contract with the Catalan Water Agency, which is renewed each January; the two town councils that share the river contribute 45,000 euros between them, a private foundation gives 60,000, and guided walks for school groups bring in the rest. Almost none of this money is committed for longer than a year. The ecologist's post has therefore been advertised as a twelve-month contract three times, and on two of those occasions the person appointed left before the contract could be renewed. Serra estimates that raising money takes about a fifth of her working year, and it comes out of the same week as everything else.

sections.heading: The next notch
sections.text: A notch two metres wide was cut in the weir in 2019, and trout were recorded above it within fourteen months. Whether to take the wall out altogether is a harder question. The channel that once fed the mill still carries water to four market gardens below the colony, and their owners, who were not consulted in 2019, have made it clear that they expect to be consulted now. The committee is divided. Some members argue that a half-restored river is not restored at all; others reply that the association's standing in the valley took ten years to build and could be spent in a single meeting. A decision has been promised for the spring of 2027.

passage.full_text:
Paragraph 1 — The weir at Colònia Nova
The mill at Colònia Nova, on the River Ter about twenty kilometres north of Vic, stopped weaving in 2011. Its weir, built in 1898 to drive the turbines, stayed where it was. In the spring of 2013 a science teacher at the local secondary school, Jordi Puig, sent his fourteen-year-olds out with thermometers as an ordinary class exercise. The water immediately above the weir turned out to be almost four degrees warmer than the water below it, and the pupils found no trout at all in the slack pool behind the wall. Puig had expected neither result. He wrote to the town council, received a polite reply, and then wrote again every month for a year. The association now known as Riu Viu was registered in 2014, largely because a permit application needed the signature of a legal body.

Paragraph 2 — Eight o'clock at the bridge
Riu Viu's week is organised around a gauge painted on the second pier of the Pont de Sant Roc. Every morning at eight, one of the volunteers reads it and posts the figure to a group message, and the same figure is copied by hand into a ledger kept in the old mill office. That number then decides what happens. Below 40 centimetres, planting is possible on the exposed gravel; above a metre, nobody enters the channel at all. Between November and January, while the trout are spawning, no work is done on the river bed whatever the gauge says. Volunteers describe this rule as inconvenient and observe it anyway. The eight o'clock reading has been missed on only nine mornings since March 2015.

Paragraph 3 — Saturday parties
The association employs two people: a coordinator, Marta Serra, and a part-time river ecologist. Everything else is done by roughly sixty volunteers, of whom perhaps twenty-five appear in any given month. Work parties meet on Saturday mornings from March to October. Their main task is cutting giant cane, an invasive reed that colonises the banks and crowds out the willow that shades the water. A party of fifteen can clear about 200 metres of bank in a morning, and the same stretch has to be revisited twice more before the roots give up. New volunteers are not sent on a training course. They are put beside somebody who has done the work before, which is how most of what Riu Viu knows is passed on.

Paragraph 4 — What the arrangement costs
The work is paid for out of about 310,000 euros a year. Rather more than half of that comes from a clearance contract with the Catalan Water Agency, which is renewed each January; the two town councils that share the river contribute 45,000 euros between them, a private foundation gives 60,000, and guided walks for school groups bring in the rest. Almost none of this money is committed for longer than a year. The ecologist's post has therefore been advertised as a twelve-month contract three times, and on two of those occasions the person appointed left before the contract could be renewed. Serra estimates that raising money takes about a fifth of her working year, and it comes out of the same week as everything else.

Paragraph 5 — The next notch
A notch two metres wide was cut in the weir in 2019, and trout were recorded above it within fourteen months. Whether to take the wall out altogether is a harder question. The channel that once fed the mill still carries water to four market gardens below the colony, and their owners, who were not consulted in 2019, have made it clear that they expect to be consulted now. The committee is divided. Some members argue that a half-restored river is not restored at all; others reply that the association's standing in the valley took ten years to build and could be spent in a single meeting. A decision has been promised for the spring of 2027.
